name: Anabolic steroid stacks (looksmaxxing)

lead: A stack is a combination of several anabolic-androgenic steroids, sometimes with growth hormone or other agents. On looksmaxxing forums, users ask for stacks that build muscle, shoulders, neck and a masculine, lean look, and some claim effects on the jaw and face.

The chain is muscle: the steroids bind and activate the androgen receptor, the same target as testosterone, which drives muscle growth and male secondary sex characteristics, producing a bigger, more masculine physique. Medicine approves steroids for conditions like low testosterone and delayed puberty, and non-medical use for appearance is documented, with studies describing most users as men around age 25. Published studies of specific stacks for facial appearance were not found.

paras: Users combine compounds for different reputed effects, run them in planned blocks, and pair them with heavy training and diet. Visible muscle changes build over weeks to months.

Medical sources list unfavourable cholesterol changes, hypertension, heart changes, suppression of the body's own testosterone production, testicular atrophy, fertility impairment, liver damage with some oral forms, acne and hair loss. In adolescents, steroids can prematurely close growth plates and stunt adult height. They are Schedule III in the US and Class C in the UK.

angle.text: Steroid combinations activate the androgen receptor to build muscle mass, neck and shoulders for a bigger, more masculine physique. Muscle gain from anabolic steroids is well documented; claims about facial bone and jaw width have not been tested.

lead: Anabolic steroid stacks are combinations of anabolic-androgenic steroids (AAS), often taken alongside other hormones or performance drugs, that users on looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums discuss for building muscle and a more masculine appearance. The chain users describe runs from androgen receptor activation to more muscle and less fat, and from there to broader shoulders, a fuller physique and a leaner look. AAS are drugs structurally related to testosterone that act by binding and activating the androgen receptor.[1]

Medical uses of AAS include testosterone replacement in men with low testosterone, inducing male puberty, treating certain anaemias and wasting conditions, and masculinising hormone therapy.[1] Non-medical use for appearance has been studied for decades: surveys in the United States describe most non-medical users as men with a median age near 25, most of them non-competitive bodybuilders or non-athletes who use the drugs for how they look.[1][2] Wikipedia estimates that 1 to 3 million Americans have used them.[2]

The word stack comes from bodybuilding culture and means using several compounds in the same period, rather than a single drug, with each compound chosen for a reputed effect. On looksmaxxing forums the topic appears in threads that ask for a stack aimed at muscle, wider clavicles, a stronger jaw or a lean look, and some of those threads are started by teenagers. This article describes the practice and the documented research; it does not give doses, cycle lengths or sourcing.

Documented adverse effects include cardiovascular and lipid changes, suppression of natural testosterone production, fertility impairment and, in adolescents, premature closure of growth plates.[1] AAS are controlled substances in the US, UK and Canada.[1] Clinical commentary in dermatology, facial plastic surgery, paediatrics and adolescent-health journals now discusses steroids and injectable peptides as part of the looksmaxxing trend among young men.[3][4][5]

paras: A stack combines more than one compound. In forum threads, members propose combinations of testosterone esters and other androgens, sometimes adding growth hormone, thyroid hormone, insulin or selective androgen receptor modulators, to pursue goals such as wider shoulders, a stronger jaw and limited water retention. Related vocabulary includes cycle (a planned period of use followed by a break) and post-cycle therapy (the use of other drugs after a cycle to help natural hormone production recover). Forum participants treat these as a shared technical vocabulary borrowed from bodybuilding, and the concepts are described in community discussions rather than in published clinical guidelines.[6][7]

The anabolic and androgenic labels date from the mid-1940s, when researchers hoped to find a testosterone derivative that built muscle without masculinising effects. Critics such as David Handelsman argue that this split is not physiologically meaningful because a single androgen receptor mediates both effects.[1] Chemists later modified testosterone in three broad ways: adding a group at the 17-alpha position so oral doses survive the liver, attaching esters so injected oil depots last longer, and altering the ring structure to change the balance of effects. This article does not describe doses or protocols.[1]

Medical use of testicle extracts began in the late nineteenth century. Adolf Butenandt isolated an androgen in 1931, Leopold Ruzicka synthesised one in 1934, and in 1935 testosterone was identified and Butenandt and Hanisch published a synthesis from cholesterol. Ruzicka and Butenandt were offered the 1939 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which the Nazi government forced Butenandt to decline; he accepted it after the war.[1] Human clinical trials with methyltestosterone and testosterone propionate began from 1937.[1]

In the 1940s and 1950s the Soviet Union and East Germany developed steroid programmes for Olympic and amateur weightlifters.[1] The CIBA company synthesised metandienone in 1955 and marketed it in the US as Dianabol from 1958, initially for burn victims and older patients, while weightlifters and other athletes used it off-label; Wikipedia describes it as the most widely used oral steroid for physique and performance purposes both historically and today.[8] The International Olympic Committee banned anabolic steroids in 1976 and began out-of-competition testing about a decade later.[1]

After the 1988 Ben Johnson doping scandal at the Seoul Olympics, the United States placed anabolic steroids in Schedule III through the Anabolic Steroids Control Act of 1990; several manufacturers then stopped selling them in the US. A 2004 amendment added prohormones, effective 2005.[1] FDA action had already ended Dianabol's US marketing in the 1980s.[8]

Approved or established uses include testosterone replacement in men with low testosterone, inducing male puberty, treating anaemias linked to leukaemia or kidney failure, supporting weight in chronic wasting, aiding recovery from burns and surgery, and masculinising therapy for transgender men.[1]

In looksmaxxing forums the aim is typically a more muscular or masculine look. One teenager asks which stack would avoid infertility and permanent hormone problems, while another thread proposes a stack for pubertymaxxing with goals including broad clavicles and a masculine face. Another poster on a bodybuilding forum, describing a first cycle, says he hopes to add about 40 pounds of muscle and finish lean.[9]

Wikipedia notes that men who use AAS non-medically often cite wanting an enhanced physical appearance, and that among 12 to 17-year-old boys one study found about 20 percent of users cited looks rather than sport.[2] Wikipedia's Looksmaxxing article places steroids, growth hormone, aromatase inhibitors and weight-loss drugs under hardmaxxing, the label for riskier medical or surgical routes.[10]

AAS are fat-soluble and cross the cell membrane to bind androgen receptors, which then move to the nucleus and change gene expression. The documented results include more muscle protein production, less muscle breakdown (partly by blocking cortisol's effects on muscle) and a shift toward muscle-cell rather than fat-cell development.[1] Oral forms are modified so the liver breaks them down more slowly, and injectable esters release the active hormone as they are hydrolysed.[1]

Users choose combinations because compounds differ in how strongly they convert to oestrogen, how they bind the receptor and how long they act, and they attribute different looks to each: bulk, dryness, hardness or vascularity. Published trials of specific multi-drug stacks for appearance outcomes were not found, so these attributions rest on user experience and bodybuilding tradition.[1][6]

Cardiovascular effects described include higher LDL and lower HDL cholesterol, hypertension, left ventricular thickening, arrhythmias, heart attack, stroke and sudden cardiac death, although the link to some heart changes is disputed.[1] Wikipedia also reports that in one study nine of ten steroid-using bodybuilders developed focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, a kidney scarring condition, and that high doses of oral AAS can cause liver damage, including peliosis hepatis.[1]

Long-term use suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, reducing natural testosterone production and causing testicular atrophy. Gynaecomastia can occur with aromatisable steroids, sperm production can be impaired, and infertility is usually reversible. Liver damage is associated mainly with oral 17-alpha-alkylated steroids, and acne and hair loss are also reported.[1] In women, effects described include irreversible voice deepening, excess body hair and menstrual changes.[1]

In adolescents, AAS can accelerate bone maturation and prematurely close growth plates, stunting adult height.[1] Psychiatric effects include aggression and mania or hypomania, with a 2005 review linking AAS to aggression, mania and, less often, psychosis; the link to depression is described as inconclusive.[1] The International Agency for Research on Cancer lists AAS as Group 2A, probably carcinogenic to humans.[1]

Long-term users are more likely to show symptoms of muscle dysmorphia, a subtype of body dysmorphic disorder in which people believe their body is too small or insufficiently muscular, and rates of the disorder are higher among steroid users.[2][11] Surveys also find that many users do not disclose their use to a physician; 56 percent in one sample had not.[1]

A sociological analysis of 8,072 comments from a large looksmaxxing forum described a community that encourages men to substantially alter their bodies and critiques physique and facial features through a masculine ideal.[12] A 2026 Missouri Medicine review lists the veterinary steroid trenbolone among the unregulated compounds promoted to young people through social media for cosmetic and athletic enhancement, and raises concerns about product contamination, inaccurate dosing and cardiovascular stress.[13]

A 2026 commentary in the Journal of Adolescent Health by Kyle Ganson, Tracy Piatkowski and Jason Nagata lists anabolic-androgenic steroid and peptide use among the risky practices that clinicians may meet in boys and young men who looksmax. The authors recommend asking about appearance concerns, screening for body dysmorphia and substance use, and using harm-reduction approaches rather than dismissing the concern.[5]

Forum members also describe steroid use in bodybuilding spaces. On T Nation, a thread about two years of trenbolone use includes replies citing the deaths of several bodybuilders from heart disease and cardiac arrest, while other threads include users who say they run high doses with manageable side effects.[6][14] One T Nation thread argues that cycling steroids is not merely renting muscle gains, reflecting a long-running debate among users about whether size is retained after stopping.[7] Another T Nation participant complains that some 14-year-olds advertise stacks to other children on TikTok.[15]

Looksmaxxing's more visible online figures have also been associated with hormone and drug use. Wikipedia reports that the streamer Braden Peters, known as Clavicular, was taken to hospital on 14 April 2026 after a livestream in which he and the influencer Androgenic described taking a combination of non-steroid drugs, and that Androgenic later defended the combination.[10] Coverage of this kind, along with warnings from clinicians, is a main way the topic has reached the general public.

AAS are Schedule III controlled substances in the United States, Class C in the United Kingdom and Schedule IV in Canada, and controlled in many other countries. Simple possession without a prescription is a federal crime in the US. In Canada buying or selling without a prescription is illegal but simple possession is not punishable. They are illegal without a prescription in Australia, Argentina, Brazil and Portugal, and readily available in Mexico and Thailand.[1] Where controlled, a black market supplies smuggled, clandestinely made or counterfeit products.[1] Most sporting bodies ban their use.[1]

Forum threads about stacks sit beside discussion of testosterone replacement therapy used by men with normal or borderline levels, selective androgen receptor modulators, growth hormone and peptides such as GHK-Cu, and of training, diet and cutting for leanness. Medical sources distinguish testosterone replacement for diagnosed hypogonadism from non-medical use for appearance.[1][16]

No studies found on steroid stacks for facial or looksmaxxing outcomes. Clinical research on individual anabolic steroids concerns medical indications such as hypogonadism, and the safety literature on non-medical use is summarised in encyclopedic sources.[1][2]

Published commentary rather than trials documents the trend: a 2026 paediatrics article titled From Mewing to Peptides describes looksmaxxing as an emerging concern in young people, a 2026 facial plastic surgery article discusses the boundary between self-enhancement and self-harm, and the 2026 Journal of Adolescent Health commentary asks for further research on who is most at risk and on short and long-term health effects.[3][4][5]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, stack threads are common, often from younger members who say they are unsatisfied with gym progress or want puberty-stage facial and shoulder changes.

claims.claim: A well-designed stack can improve facial masculinity and skeletal width during or after puberty.
Stacks can be chosen to avoid infertility and hormone shutdown.
Adding growth hormone, thyroid hormone, insulin or SARMs to a stack improves the result.
Stacking several compounds lets users avoid the side effects of a single drug.
Steroids are the main route to a physique that diet and training alone cannot reach.
Muscle gained on a cycle can be kept after stopping.
Teenagers can use steroids to change puberty-stage features such as shoulders and jaw.
Heavy steroid use is manageable with monitoring and careful compound choice.
